, to protect a huge table: Chapter 14.)
The dbt Labs project-structure guide, and most real projects, start from one materialization per layer (Chapter 9 explains the layers):

blocks.alt: One materialization per layer, from left to right: Sources (raw tables loaded by others, not built by dbt) → Staging (rename, cast, light cleaning: view) → Intermediate (reusable steps, joins, re-graining: ephemeral or view) → Marts (business entities read by people: table, later incremental) → Consumers (BI dashboards, notebooks, apps).

c: The logic is light, nobody outside the team queries it, and a view costs no storage and is always as fresh as the raw data.
Ephemeral keeps the warehouse clean; a view (often in a separate schema with limited access) is easier to debug. Our project uses both: ephemeral for the tiny
for the bigger intermediate models of Chapter 9.
BI tools read them many times a day; the heavy work should happen once, during the run.
dbt Labs' advice can be summed up as:
start with a view; when it is too slow to query, make it a table; when the table is too slow to build, make it incremental.
Do not start with incremental models "just in case": they add complexity (strategies, filters, full refreshes) that you only want when the time or the cost is a real problem.
One more warning sign: a long chain of views (or ephemeral models) on top of each other. Each read must compute the whole chain. The
package from dbt Labs flags chains of more than five non-physical models (its default threshold). Turning one model in the middle of the chain into a table usually fixes it.
